risk_flags.description: The diagnosis of type 2 diabetes is asserted, but the clinical picture (ketosis, acidosis) may be more consistent with type 1 diabetes or DKA. The diagnosis is not fully supported by the evidence without further clarification.

specialist_trace.rationale: To ensure accurate coding, the provider must explicitly document the acute metabolic decompensation as diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) or a related acidosis/ketosis syndrome, and clarify whether this presentation is consistent with type 2 diabetes with ketosis-prone features or an alternative type (e.g., type 1, LADA). Additionally, the chart should include a clinical statement linking the abnormal labs (pH, HCO3, ketones, glucose, HbA1c) to the diagnosis and outline the planned workup (e.g., autoantibody testing, C-peptide) and treatment (e.g., insulin protocol), as this specificity is essential for correct code assignment and severity capture.

I do not have live PubMed search access, so I cannot provide verified PMIDs. However, based on established literature, ketosis-prone diabetes in a 45-year-old with severe hyperglycemia (HbA1c 11.2%) and metabolic acidosis (pH 7.30, HCO3 16) warrants evaluation for autoimmune (type 1/LADA) or ketosis-prone type 2 diabetes, as up to 10–20% of phenotypic type 2 patients with DKA have positive islet autoantibodies (e.g., GAD65) and require insulin. The chart gap is clinically significant: without specifying diabetes type or documenting a workup plan (autoantibodies, C-peptide, insulin initiation), the risk of misclassification and inappropriate oral-agent-only therapy is high. I recommend explicitly documenting "DKA (ketosis-prone diabetes, type to be determined)" and ordering GAD65, IA-2, and C-peptide to guide long-term therapy.
